idiom_name: module of functions over an opaque struct (+ explicit ops table for the capability)
implementation_notes: C has no methods, so the servant is a set of functions in one translation unit that take a pointer to the serviced object, whose representation stays hidden in its own module; the capability interface becomes an explicit contract - a struct of function pointers (an ops table) or a tag plus switch, because C has neither classes nor structural typing. The canonical stdlib servant is qsort: it knows nothing about the element type, requires the caller to supply the comparison capability as a callback, and provides the algorithm once. Because there is no method dispatch to remove, the servant form is not a choice in C - the only decision is how the capability travels: an ops table alongside the object (general, one vtable per serviced type), a caller-supplied callback (the qsort shape, best for one operation), or a tag plus switch (simplest, and the point where the servant starts guessing types). Keep the ops table if several servants should share the same requirement.
pitfalls: The capability must be passed explicitly at every call, so its lifetime must outlive the object: a function-pointer table pointing at code (or context) that is gone is a dangling vtable with no runtime check.
void * erases type safety - a mismatched ops table is only caught when it crashes; keep object and ops together in one struct if many call sites pass the pair around.
A callback that needs state forces either a global (thread-unsafe with a shared servant) or a context parameter (qsort_r) - never smuggle state through statics.
sources: cppreference, qsort - the servant/algorithm with a caller-supplied comparison capability and an opaque element type; https://en.cppreference.com/c/algorithm/qsort

POSIX.1-2024, qsort/qsort_r - states that a comparator needing extra state otherwise needs globals, and that qsort_r exists to avoid them; https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9799919799/functions/qsort.html
